modalities.whatYouDo: Six to twelve people meet weekly for 90 minutes over six weeks with a facilitator who supplies materials and steps, from cutting and gluing to stringing and tuning, while members swap stories about music in their lives. In the last session everyone plays their homemade instruments together, roughly but proudly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who thrive on goals and making things, and anyone who wants a structured, sociable commitment that ends in something to keep.
modalities.cautions: Tools, glue and strings need care, so the facilitator should teach safe use, provide eye protection where needed and adapt tasks for people with limited hand strength. Keep the playing volume comfortable.
modalities.tweet: Six weeks, a small group, a box of materials: everyone builds a box guitar or thumb piano, then the group plays them together, badly and proudly. A hypothetical project for people who need a goal and a team: Instrument Build-Along.

modalities.name: Doorstep Serenade
modalities.tagline: Learning one short piece to sing or play for one person.
modalities.whatItIs: Doorstep Serenade is a new concept in which a small group, led by someone who can teach a song, picks one person, such as a housebound neighbor or a friend having a hard week, finds out which song mattered to them in the past, learns it and sings it at their door. Metta and jhana meditation cultivate goodwill silently and alone; music pushed the other way makes goodwill audible, rehearsed with others and given to a real person through a song from their own history.
modalities.coreIdea: Turning a wish for someone into a real song from their past, sung at their door, can make kindness something both sides can hear.
modalities.whatYouDo: The leader asks the person, or someone close to them, which song they loved when they were younger, teaches it to three to eight people over an evening or two and arranges a time. The group gathers at the door, sings it once and leaves unless invited to stay.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find silent, inward practices lonely, and anyone who wants a warm, practical way to show care together with others.
modalities.cautions: Always ask first, since a surprise performance can be unwelcome or alarming, keep it short and respect neighbors and quiet hours. Songs can stir strong feelings for the listener, so let them choose whether to come to the door.
modalities.tweet: Find out which song a housebound neighbor loved when they were young. Ask first, learn it with a few friends and a leader, then sing it once at their door. Doorstep Serenade, a new concept for kindness you can actually hear.

modalities.name: Tune Telephone
modalities.tagline: A melody passed ear to ear, changing as it goes.
modalities.whatItIs: Tune Telephone is a new concept for a lively group game in which a short melody, often one someone remembers from childhood, is hummed quietly into the next person's ear and passed down a line until the last person sings out whatever it has become. Vipassana watches experience with silent, still precision; this lies past music in the other direction, where tunes are played with, misheard, invented and changed on purpose.
modalities.coreIdea: Watching a melody mutate as it passes from person to person turns memory and imagination into shared play, where getting it wrong is the fun.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to fifteen people stand in a line, and the first hums a five-second tune to the second, who hums what they heard to the third, and so on to the end, where the last person sings it out loud and the first sings the original. A host keeps the rounds moving for about an hour, and anyone can bring a tune.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find meditation too passive or solemn, and groups who like laughter, games and a little creative chaos.
modalities.cautions: Humming close to someone's ear means agreeing on comfort first, so anyone can whisper from a step away or simply watch. Keep the final sung-out versions at a comfortable volume.
modalities.tweet: Remember the telephone game? Do it with a tune: hum five seconds of melody into the next person's ear, pass it down the line and hear what it turned into. Tune Telephone, a new idea that rewards getting it wrong.

modalities.name: Lullaby Hour for Adults
modalities.tagline: Slow, soft songs sung in dim light, with nothing to do.
modalities.whatItIs: Lullaby Hour for Adults is a new concept for calm evenings in which people sit or lie in dim light while one or two people softly sing or play slow songs, including lullabies some remember from childhood. HIIT is all effort and activation; this takes music to the opposite extreme, using it for slowness, softness and rest.
modalities.coreIdea: Slow, quiet songs, heard lying down in company, invite the body toward rest the way a lullaby does, without anything being asked of the listener.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to fifteen people bring cushions or mats to a dim room, and a host who knows a store of gentle songs sings softly or plays a quiet instrument for about an hour, with long pauses between songs. Listeners can hum along, ask for a song from their own childhood or simply drift, and the hour ends in silence.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always switched on and find it hard to wind down, and anyone who misses being sung to.
modalities.cautions: Lullabies and childhood songs can bring up tender or painful memories, so anyone can leave or sit apart, and lasting distress is worth discussing with a therapist. Keep the room safe for people who may doze off, and keep the volume soft.
modalities.tweet: New idea for people who never switch off: Lullaby Hour for Adults. Dim lights, cushions on the floor, someone softly singing slow songs and old lullabies for an hour. Hum along or just drift. When did someone last sing you to rest? 🌙

modalities.name: Solo Reverie Listening
modalities.tagline: Alone with slow music, letting memories drift, then writing a little.
modalities.whatItIs: Solo Reverie Listening is a proposed practice of sitting alone and still with a few pieces of slow music while memories and images drift through, then writing a few lines about what came. It sits beyond music on the far side from team sport: no team, no speed and no shouting, just one person, quiet music and an inner world.
modalities.coreIdea: Slow music heard in solitude can open a gentle reverie in which memories surface and settle at their own pace, with no one guiding or responding.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the basics once from a music therapist or experienced teacher, including how to choose suitable pieces and when to stop, you sit alone with headphones at a moderate volume and listen to three slow pieces, about 20 minutes, with your eyes closed. Afterward you write freely for five minutes, then do something ordinary such as making tea.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are drawn to music and memory but prefer to reflect alone, and anyone who wants a quiet ritual away from busy, social days.
modalities.cautions: Reverie can bring up painful memories, and sad music can deepen a low mood for people prone to rumination, so choose pieces with care, stop if you feel worse and talk to a therapist if heavy memories keep returning. Keep headphone volume moderate to protect your hearing.
modalities.tweet: Sit alone, eyes closed, with three slow pieces of music for 20 minutes and let memories drift in and out. Then write a few lines and make tea. Solo Reverie Listening is an untested concept, best learned from a music therapist first.

modalities.name: Music Life Interviews
modalities.tagline: Pairs interviewing each other about the music in their lives.
modalities.whatItIs: Music Life Interviews is a proposed practice for facilitated groups in which people pair up and, using a set of question cards, interview each other about the music in their lives, such as the first record they owned or the song that got them through a hard year, with no music played at all. Endurance training is solitary, self-led and physical; music on the far side from it becomes seated, guided and social, and the effort goes into listening to another person's story.
modalities.coreIdea: Being asked careful questions about your musical life, by someone who really listens, can gently open personal history in a structured, mutual way.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to sixteen people meet for about 90 minutes with a facilitator who explains the cards and keeps time, and each pair spends 20 minutes on each person, then the group shares one surprising answer each. People choose which cards to answer and can pass on any.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy music and conversation, and anyone who would find open-ended talk about the past too much without a structure.
modalities.cautions: Questions about the past can stir grief or difficult memories, so anyone can pass, and the facilitator should know how to respond gently. If memories become heavy or keep returning afterward, talk to a therapist.
modalities.tweet: What was the first record you owned? Which song got you through your worst year? Pair up, use question cards and interview each other about the music in your lives. Music Life Interviews is an untested format, no playlist required.

modalities.name: Half-Remembered Songs
modalities.tagline: Piecing together songs you only half remember, with others' help.
modalities.whatItIs: Half-Remembered Songs is a speculative practice of a loose group helping each other rebuild songs that members only half remember, from a fragment of a tune or a single line. Strength training is effort, structure and measurable progress; in this corner of music beyond the anchor, nobody performs, nothing is measured, and imperfect recall is the whole point.
modalities.coreIdea: Piecing a lost song back together is a gentle, shared puzzle that reaches into personal history without any pressure to get it right.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to twelve people sit in a comfortable room for about 90 minutes, and someone hums or describes a song they half remember, perhaps from a school bus, a grandparent or an old radio. Others offer missing lines or guesses, a host with a phone or songbook may help track it down, and the group sings whatever version emerges.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they always have to perform or be good at things, older adults who enjoy reminiscing, and anyone who loves a musical puzzle.
modalities.cautions: Old songs can bring back people and times that are gone, so grief may surface; anyone can step out or simply listen, and if memories become heavy or keep returning, talk to a therapist. For people living with memory loss, sessions should be gentle and led by someone experienced.
modalities.tweet: Ever had a scrap of a tune you can't place? Hum it to a room of friends, from a school bus or a grandparent's kitchen, and let them help piece it back together. Nobody performs, nothing is measured. Half-Remembered Songs: a new idea.

modalities.name: Score Your Own Day
modalities.tagline: Imagining a film soundtrack for the ordinary scenes of your day.
modalities.whatItIs: Score Your Own Day is a new concept for two people who share a day, such as partners, flatmates or friends, choosing or imagining a soundtrack for its ordinary scenes, as if the day were a film, and humming or playing it as they go. Animal-assisted therapy rests on a real animal and a professional in the room; music pushed away from it runs on imagination, and the two of you lead yourselves.
modalities.coreIdea: Giving everyday scenes a soundtrack changes how they feel, and choosing that soundtrack yourself is a way of playing with mood and meaning.
modalities.whatYouDo: In the morning you agree on three shared scenes ahead, such as the walk to the shop, washing up together and cooking dinner, and each of you picks or imagines music for them, from heroic to peaceful. You hum it, play it quietly or share a speaker during the scene, and in the evening you compare which soundtrack fitted best.
modalities.whoItsFor: Partners, friends or flatmates who find shared routines dull, and imaginative people who love film and music.
modalities.cautions: Never wear headphones where you need to hear traffic, and keep the volume moderate. Choosing mostly sad soundtracks can pull a low mood further down, so if that happens, pick lighter music or talk to someone.
modalities.tweet: Imagine your shared day had a film score. With a partner or flatmate, pick soundtracks for three ordinary scenes (washing up, the walk to the shop, cooking) and hum them as you go. Score Your Own Day is a new idea. Heroic dishes, anyone? 🎬

modalities.name: Everything Must Be Sung
modalities.tagline: A loose evening where every ordinary remark must be sung.
modalities.whatItIs: Everything Must Be Sung is a speculative practice for lively gatherings in which, for half an hour at a time, everything anyone says has to be sung, from passing the salt to describing their week, in made-up melodies. Qigong repeats slow, set forms with regulated breath; at the far opposite edge of music from it, nothing is set, the energy is high, and imagination and old memories surface in song.
modalities.coreIdea: Singing ordinary speech turns everyday talk into play, and the absurdity may loosen people up enough to share things they would not just say.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to twelve people share a meal or a cup of tea, and a host sets a timer and announces that, until it rings, every remark must be sung, operatically, in a pop style or however it comes out. Between rounds people talk normally and laugh about it, and the host may suggest a theme for the next round, such as a childhood holiday.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like laughter and play, and anyone who feels stiff or self-conscious in ordinary conversation.
modalities.cautions: Singing in front of others can feel exposing, so anyone can whisper-sing or just listen, and the group keeps the mood kind. Keep the volume reasonable for neighbors.
modalities.tweet: For thirty minutes, everything you say has to be sung. Pass the salt? Aria. How was work? Power ballad. A speculative dinner game for anyone who feels stiff in ordinary conversation: Everything Must Be Sung.

modalities.name: Lessons by Letter
modalities.tagline: Practicing alone and getting a teacher's notes only by letter.
modalities.whatItIs: Lessons by Letter is a new concept for private, structured music practice in which you never play in front of anyone: each week you record a short attempt at a piece you care about and send it to a teacher, who replies only with brief written notes. Socializing builds on live company; this pushes music the opposite way, toward solitary practice guided at a distance.
modalities.coreIdea: Practicing with nobody in the room, but with steady written guidance, gives the calm of solitude and the direction of a teacher at the same time.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a piece that matters to you, practice alone for 15 minutes a day, and once a week record a single take and send it. The teacher writes back a few lines, such as one thing that improved and one thing to try, and you work on that alone the following week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel too shy to play for anyone, and anyone who prefers quiet, private progress to lessons or groups.
modalities.cautions: Ease in with short sessions and warm-ups to avoid strain in the hands, wrists, lips or voice. A piece tied to someone or something from your past can stir strong feelings, so talk with someone you trust or a therapist if it weighs on you.
modalities.tweet: Too shy to play for anyone? Practice alone, record one take a week, send it to a teacher, get back three lines of notes. Nobody ever watches you play. Lessons by Letter is a speculative format for very private progress.

modalities.name: Loop by Loop
modalities.tagline: A guided indoor course building one layered loop track about a time.
modalities.whatItIs: Loop by Loop is a proposed indoor course in which a small group, guided by a facilitator, spends six weeks building one short track each on a laptop or phone, layering simple loops into a sound portrait of a period of their own life. Nature walks are open, self-led and outdoors; music past the far side from them becomes structured, guided, imaginative work at a desk, reaching into personal history.
modalities.coreIdea: Building a piece one loop at a time lets you shape a memory into sound step by step, with a finished result and no need to sing or play live.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to ten people meet weekly for two hours, and the facilitator teaches one simple step each week, such as recording a sound, looping a beat, adding a hummed melody and balancing the layers, while each person works on their own track. In the last session everyone plays their track for the group, or chooses to keep it private.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a creative, structured project with a clear end point, and anyone curious about making music with technology rather than instruments.
modalities.cautions: Portraits of hard periods can bring up painful memories, so participants choose which time to work on, and the facilitator should know when to suggest professional support; anyone working through trauma should do that with a trained therapist. Keep headphone volume moderate and take screen breaks.
modalities.tweet: One laptop, six weeks, one short track: layer a hummed melody, a looped beat and a recorded sound into a portrait of a time in your life. Loop by Loop, an untested course for people who'd rather build music than perform it.

modalities.name: Soundscapes of Memory
modalities.tagline: A group recreating a remembered place in sound, voices and objects.
modalities.whatItIs: Soundscapes of Memory is a new concept for guided group sessions in which people recreate the sounds of a remembered place, such as a grandmother's kitchen or a school playground, using voices, everyday objects and simple instruments. Sensory mindfulness gives quiet attention to what the senses meet right now; music pushed away from it turns to imagination, memory and lively group play.
modalities.coreIdea: Rebuilding a place in sound brings memory and imagination together, and doing it as a group turns one person's past into a shared, lively creation.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a session of about 90 minutes, a facilitator helps one volunteer describe a place from their past, and the group works out how to make its sounds, such as clattering pans, a kettle, distant traffic or a voice calling. The volunteer listens with eyes closed while the group performs the soundscape, then says what came back, and the next person takes a turn.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy imagination and group play, and anyone who would like to revisit a meaningful place from their past with others.
modalities.cautions: Recreated places can bring back strong feelings, both warm and painful, so volunteers choose their place and can stop at any time, and the facilitator should know when to pause. Difficult or traumatic places belong in work with a trained therapist, not in a group game.
modalities.tweet: One person describes a place from their past, a grandmother's kitchen or a school playground, and the group recreates it in sound with voices, pans and a kettle while they listen, eyes closed. New and untested: Soundscapes of Memory.
